Views on the future of business 
The following is a summary from an article in The Economist, which I found interesting. It's not my usual style but it was worth reading.
"Businesses are changing their ways and becoming more like charities"
In 2010, when he took over as chief executive at Unilever (the maker of Dove soap), Paul Polman made two pledges: to cut his company’s environmental footprint by half within five years; and to double its profits while doing so. He has kept both promises – with one exception. Profits have risen only slightly since then, though they were already high before Mr Polman arrived. But that does not matter much because “we don’t do profit for the sake of making money”, says Mr Polman. Instead, he wants shareholders to be happy about how well employees treat customers or suppliers, whether communities benefit from local projects or consumers get value-for-money products.
Mr Polman believes this approach will help him achieve another goal too: doubling sales growth year-on-year between now and 2025. That would make Unilever bigger than Procter & Gamble, Pepsico or Nestlé combined. To reach such heights requires innovation across all areas of operations, including supply chains, manufacturing processes and marketing techniques. In other words, businesses need to become less focused on short-term financial gains and start thinking long term instead."
I think there may be some truth here - especially if you look back through history where companies used to focus purely on shareholder returns rather than any social responsibility towards society etc...

Astronomers have found a way to explain why some stars are spinning faster than others.
Stars rotate because they were formed from collapsing clouds that spun around their own axes as gravity pulled them inwards. But astronomers had long been puzzled about how this rotation could be maintained over billions of years without slowing down or stopping altogether – especially since most galaxies appear to contain many more slowly rotating objects than fast ones.
Now an international team has come up with what it believes is one possible explanation for these discrepancies between star spin rates and galaxy structure. It suggests that when two gas-rich spiral galaxies collide head-on at high speed, gravitational waves generated during the collision can slow both spirals' spins until eventually only very few remain rapidly rotating after such encounters.
This idea was first proposed back in 1974 but its implications remained unclear due to lack of data. Now however, using computer simulations based upon observations made through NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope, researchers led by Michael Fall of San Francisco State University say there may well be enough evidence out there now to support the hypothesis.
"Gravitational wave emission should cause all systems involved in collisions like those we see today to lose angular momentum," says co-author Mark Krumholz of Princeton University in New Jersey. He adds that if true then our Milky Way Galaxy itself might once have contained several hundred times more rapid rotators before being slowed down by interactions with other nearby galaxies.
If so, he notes, this would help account not just for the large number of low-spinning objects observed within individual galaxies, but also for the fact that almost every single object seen outside any given system appears to move relatively quickly compared to everything else inside it.
"This result provides strong motivation for future searches aimed specifically at detecting gravitational radiation emitted following close galactic mergers."
For further information contact M.Krumholtz@princeton.edu .

But astronomers had long been puzzled about how this rotation could be maintained over billions of years without slowing down or stopping altogether – especially since most galaxies appear to contain many more slowly rotating objects than fast ones.
Now an international team has come up with what it believes is one possible explanation for these discrepancies between star spin rates and galaxy structure. It suggests that when two gas-rich spiral galaxies collide head-on at high speed, gravitational waves generated during the collision can slow both spirals' spins until eventually only very few remain rapidly rotating after such encounters.
This idea was first proposed back in 1974 but its implications remained unclear due to lack of data. Now however, using computer simulations based upon observations made through NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope, researchers led by Michael Fall of San Francisco State University say there may well be enough evidence out there now to support the hypothesis.
"Gravitational wave emission should cause all systems involved in collisions like those we see today to lose angular momentum," says co-author Mark Krumholz of Princeton University in New Jersey. He adds that if true then our Milky Way Galaxy itself might once have contained several hundred times more rapid rotators before being slowed down by interactions with other nearby galaxies.
If so, he notes, this would help account not just for the large number of low-spinning objects observed within individual galaxies, but also for the fact that almost every single object seen outside any given system appears to move relatively quickly compared to everything else inside it.
"This result provides strong motivation for future searches aimed specifically at detecting gravitational radiation emitted following close galactic mergers."

1. KOSPI closes up as investors eye Fed policy meeting next month
By Kim Hyun-chae - Staff Reporter / Business Section
Stocks closed higher Friday after two straight sessions of losses amid expectations that the Federal Reserve will announce its decision regarding interest rates during its upcoming monthly monetary-policy committee meetings later this month.
In addition, foreign institutional investment was seen flowing into local stocks due mainly to positive sentiment over China’s economic growth prospects ahead of Beijing’s annual legislative session starting Monday.
At closing bell, the benchmark Kospi rose 3.5 points, or 0.4 percent, to close above the psychologically important level of 900 while the broader Kosdaq index gained 6.7 points, or less than one-tenth of a percentage point, ending below the key mark of 600.
“Investors were cautious but not overly concerned,” said Lee Seung-hoon, analyst at Mirae Asset Daewoo Securities Co., adding “the market has been trading within narrow ranges.”
“The recent volatility may be attributed to uncertainty surrounding whether the central bank would raise short-term lending rate again soon given signs showing inflationary pressures easing off slightly recently.” he added.
On Thursday, the Bank of Korea raised overnight borrowing costs by five basis points to three-quarters of a per cent, citing rising prices of imported oil products such as gasoline which have pushed consumer price increases upwardly since late November.
But analysts say it remains unclear if further hikes could come anytime soon because domestic demand appears sluggish despite strong exports performance so far this quarter thanks largely to robust overseas sales of memory chips made locally.
Meanwhile, Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao announced plans Wednesday to boost spending on infrastructure projects worth $586 billion through fiscal stimulus measures aimed primarily at boosting consumption among ordinary citizens who account for nearly half of total GDP output.
Wen also pledged to cut taxes across-the-board including those levied against small businesses whose owners make only around minimum wage income levels.
Analysts expect these moves should help stabilize China’s slowing down economy although they warn there still remain risks associated with high debt burdens held mostly by state-owned enterprises.
As concerns lingered over global financial markets’ health especially Europe where Greece faces mounting pressure to secure bailout funds needed to avoid defaulting payments toward international lenders, major Asian stock indexes ended lower except Japan’s Nikkei average which advanced sharply led by gains recorded by exporters like Sony Corp. and Panasonic Corp.
Among blue chip shares listed here, Samsung Electronics Co.’s gain came partly backed by reports saying Apple Inc. had ordered additional supplies of components used in making iPhones and iPads.
Samsung Heavy Industries Ltd. jumped almost four percent even though no official confirmation yet emerged confirming media speculation earlier suggesting shipbuilder might win orders totaling hundreds of millions dollars from Saudi Arabia’s national airline company Saudia Airlines.
Also helping lift the tech giant’s fortunes was upbeat outlook provided by rival Hyundai Motor Group affiliates Hyundai Mobis Co. and Kia Motors Corp. both reporting better-than expected earnings results for fourth-quarter period just concluded.
Hyundai Mobis posted net profit of W50.8 billion ($46 million), beating consensus estimates calling for profits ranging between W45 billion-$48 billion according to Thomson Reuters I/B/E/S data compiled Tuesday morning.
Net operating margin stood at eight-point-six-one-percent compared to seven-per-cent reported previously.
Earnings excluding non-recurring items amounted to W55.9 billion versus forecasts pegged at W52 billion-W54 billion range.
Operating revenue increased nine-and-a-half-percent sequentially to reach W1 trillion marking highest-ever quarterly figure ever achieved thus far.
Sales volume grew six-and-three-fourths-percent driven chiefly by auto parts business segment posting double-digit increase in shipments.
Revenue generated via export channel accounted for roughly eighty-five-percent of overall tally.
“We’ve managed to achieve record-high profitability without any significant cost-cutting efforts taken” CEO Park Jong-won told reporters when announcing preliminary figures early afternoon.
He noted however that firm remained committed towards achieving target set out under medium-to-long term plan unveiled back then aiming to post combined revenues exceeding ten-trillion won annually along with healthy margins standing northward of twelve-points-two-percent.
Park went onto add his outfit planned to invest heavily in research development activities targeting new technologies likely to emerge going forward particularly ones related to electric vehicles EVs and fuel cell systems FCVs.
Separately, Kia Motors saw bottom-line rise twenty-eight-billion won

Stocks closed higher Friday after two straight sessions of losses amid expectations that the Federal Reserve will announce its decision regarding interest rates during its upcoming monthly monetary-policy committee meetings later this month.
In addition, foreign institutional investment was seen flowing into local stocks due mainly to positive sentiment over China’s economic growth prospects ahead of Beijing’s annual legislative session starting Monday.
At closing bell, the benchmark Kospi rose 3.5 points, or 0.4 percent, to close above the psychologically important level of 900 while the broader Kosdaq index gained 6.7 points, or less than one-tenth of a percentage point, ending below the key mark of 600.
“Investors were cautious but not overly concerned,” said Lee Seung-hoon, analyst at Mirae Asset Daewoo Securities Co., adding “the market has been trading within narrow ranges.”
“The recent volatility may be attributed to uncertainty surrounding whether the central bank would raise short-term lending rate again soon given signs showing inflationary pressures easing off slightly recently.” he added.
On Thursday, the Bank of Korea raised overnight borrowing costs by five basis points to three-quarters of a per cent, citing rising prices of imported oil products such as gasoline which have pushed consumer price increases upwardly since late November.
But analysts say it remains unclear if further hikes could come anytime soon because domestic demand appears sluggish despite strong exports performance so far this quarter thanks largely to robust overseas sales of memory chips made locally.
Meanwhile, Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao announced plans Wednesday to boost spending on infrastructure projects worth $586 billion through fiscal stimulus measures aimed primarily at boosting consumption among ordinary citizens who account for nearly half of total GDP output.
Wen also pledged to cut taxes across-the-board including those levied against small businesses whose owners make only around minimum wage income levels.
Analysts expect these moves should help stabilize China’s slowing down economy although they warn there still remain risks associated with high debt burdens held mostly by state-owned enterprises.
As concerns lingered over global financial markets’ health especially Europe where Greece faces mounting pressure to secure bailout funds needed to avoid defaulting payments toward international lenders, major Asian stock indexes ended lower except Japan’s Nikkei average which advanced sharply led by gains recorded by exporters like Sony Corp. and Panasonic Corp.
Among blue chip shares listed here, Samsung Electronics Co.’s gain came partly backed by reports saying Apple Inc. had ordered additional supplies of components used in making iPhones and iPads.
Samsung Heavy Industries Ltd. jumped almost four percent even though no official confirmation yet emerged confirming media speculation earlier suggesting shipbuilder might win orders totaling hundreds of millions dollars from Saudi Arabia’s national airline company Saudia Airlines.
Also helping lift the tech giant’s fortunes was upbeat outlook provided by rival Hyundai Motor Group affiliates Hyundai Mobis Co. and Kia Motors Corp. both reporting better-than expected earnings results for fourth-quarter period just concluded.
Hyundai Mobis posted net profit of W50.8 billion ($46 million), beating consensus estimates calling for profits ranging between W45 billion-$48 billion according to Thomson Reuters I/B/E/S data compiled Tuesday morning.
Net operating margin stood at eight-point-six-one-percent compared to seven-per-cent reported previously.
Earnings excluding non-recurring items amounted to W55.9 billion versus forecasts pegged at W52 billion-W54 billion range.
Operating revenue increased nine-and-a-half-percent sequentially to reach W1 trillion marking highest-ever quarterly figure ever achieved thus far.
Sales volume grew six-and-three-fourths-percent driven chiefly by auto parts business segment posting double-digit increase in shipments.
Revenue generated via export channel accounted for roughly eighty-five-percent of overall tally.
“We’ve managed to achieve record-high profitability without any significant cost-cutting efforts taken” CEO Park Jong-won told reporters when announcing preliminary figures early afternoon.
He noted however that firm remained committed towards achieving target set out under medium-to-long term plan unveiled back then aiming to post combined revenues exceeding ten-trillion won annually along with healthy margins standing northward of twelve-points-two-percent.
Park went onto add his outfit planned to invest heavily in research development activities targeting new technologies likely to emerge going forward particularly ones related to electric vehicles EVs and fuel cell systems FCVs.
Separately, Kia Motors saw bottom-line rise twenty-eight-billion won

[ANS] A New Way To Make Solar Cells - 2007-10-30
A team of researchers at the University of California, Riverside has developed a method for making thin-film photovoltaic devices that could lead to cheaper and more efficient solar energy.
The research was published in Nature Materials on Oct. 21 by UC Riverside professor Hua Zhang , his graduate student Yujie Rong (first author), postdoctoral researcher Xiangfeng Duan from Peking University, China; and their colleagues: Zhenan Bao, associate director of Stanford's Institute for Polymer Research ; Xiaoyang Zhuo, assistant professor of chemistry at UCR; and Qian Wang, an undergraduate physics major who is now working as a scientist with Hewlett-Packard Co., Palo Alto, Calif .
Zhang said he hopes this work will help bring down costs associated with producing silicon-based PVs -- which are currently used commercially but have high manufacturing cost because they require large amounts of expensive materials such as polysilicon or glass substrates . The technology also requires complex processing steps involving multiple masks during fabrication.
In contrast, the technique described here uses inexpensive copper foil instead of costly glasses or polymers as substrate material. It can be fabricated using simple printing techniques without any mask required. This makes it possible to produce flexible plastic films containing thousands of tiny nanowires made up entirely of semiconductor compounds called chalcogenides.
Chalcogens include sulfur, selenium and tellurium, all elements found naturally occurring within Earth ' s crust. They form crystals when combined with other metals like cadmium, zinc, tin and indium. These semimetallic alloys exhibit unique electrical properties due to quantum confinement effects caused by small size of these nanostructures.

The research by scientists at Columbia University in New York found an association between having one or two copies of the gene for red-green blindness — which affects about 12 percent of men but only slightly fewer women worldwide — and higher rates of autistic behavior among their offspring compared with other families.
Autism spectrum disorders include Asperger's syndrome as well as classic forms such as Kanner's disorder named after its discoverer Leo Kanner, whose son was diagnosed on his own child psychologist's advice when he was just 11 months old.
"Color vision deficiency has been associated previously with increased risk of schizophrenia," said lead author Dr. Daniel Geschwind from UCLA School of Medicine in Los Angeles. "We were interested if there might also be some link between these conditions."
He added it could not yet be determined whether being genetically predisposed toward either disease increases susceptibility to both because they share common symptoms like social withdrawal and repetitive behaviors.
In addition, researchers did find no evidence linking blue-yellow visual impairment to any increase in autism cases.
For the report published Wednesday online ahead of print publication in Archives of General Psychiatry, investigators analyzed data collected over several years involving nearly 400 pairs of parents and siblings living across California.
They looked specifically at how many had inherited genes coding for defective versions of three different proteins involved in transmitting signals within nerve cells called neurotransmitters.
One protein affected by mutations linked to red-greensightlessness codes for rhodopsin; another encodes opsin while still others code for arrestins.
Researchers used DNA samples taken during routine health screenings provided through state-mandated newborn screening programs run jointly by public hospitals and private laboratories throughout most states.
Among all participants studied, each pair averaged four family members per generation including grandparents, uncles, cousins and so forth back five generations into history.
Of them, almost half carried mutant alleles affecting opsine production responsible for normal perception of colors ranging from greenish yellow to reddish brown hues known collectively as trichromatic vision.
About twice as often, however, subjects possessed mutated variants encoding arrestedyns thought to play roles regulating activity levels inside neurons.
And roughly eight times out of ten, individuals carrying defects causing reduced ability to perceive differences in shades of gray coded for abnormality in rhodopshin expression.
Overall, results showed significantly greater odds of inheriting multiple types of altered allele combinations related to impaired function of various brain chemicals implicated in mental illness.
But perhaps surprisingly, none appeared connected directly to heightened risks of developing full-blown psychiatric problems themselves despite previous studies suggesting otherwise.
Instead, what seemed significant instead was finding links tying specific variations in chromosome-linked material influencing development of certain organs and tissues to elevated likelihoods of producing kids later afflicted with behavioral abnormalities similar to those seen in patients suffering from autism.
"This work provides further support for our hypothesis that chromosomal imbalance contributes to neurodevelopmental diseases," wrote co-author Dr. Eric Morrow from Children's Hospital Boston in Massachusetts commenting separately via e-mail.
"The findings suggest that alterations in neuronal signaling pathways can contribute to developmental disabilities even though the individual does not suffer from overt neurological dysfunction himself/herself."

The first woman to fly into orbit was Valentina Tereshkova of the Soviet Union. She flew on Vostok 6 and spent three days circling Earth before returning safely back home. Her flight made history as a milestone for female astronauts but also because it marked an important step forward toward international cooperation between nations that had been locked in conflict during World War II. 10.1126/
science.11936542
Women are underrepresented at all levels and stages within science,
and this disparity persists despite decades-long efforts to increase their participation (see page 1233). In a study that examined data from more than half-a-million researchers worldwide over an almost decade-and-half period between 1997 and 2010, we found no evidence for any improvement or change in gender balance across different fields of research; rather there was little variation among countries with respect to women's representation as well as stagnation overall. We also show how these trends have affected career progression through analysis of promotion rates based on sex and field of work. Our findings suggest that current policies aimed at increasing female presence may not be effective unless they address structural barriers such as unequal access to resources and opportunities. This article describes our methods and results along with policy implications derived from them.

In contrast, the technique described here uses inexpensive copper foil instead of costly glasses or polymers as substrate material. It can be fabricated using simple printing techniques without any mask required. This makes it possible to produce flexible plastic films containing thousands of tiny nanowires made up entirely of semiconductor compounds called chalcogenides.
Chalcogens include sulfur, selenium and tellurium, all elements found naturally occurring within Earth ' s crust. They form crystals when combined with other metals like cadmium, zinc, tin and indium. These semimetallic alloys exhibit unique electrical properties due to quantum confinement effects caused by small size of these nanostructures.

AFTER a decade in which America's power has been challenged from without 
and within, it seems that its moment may have come again. In recent weeks,
the United States has shown itself to be not only strong but also wise--in 
its handling both of Iraq and North Korea; as well as generous towards other 
nations such as China or India who are trying hard to catch up with them;
as well as tough-minded about those like Iran whose ambitions threaten their own security.
America can now look forward confidently into an era when they will once more play leading roles at home and abroad.
In this issue we examine how far these changes might affect American life over coming years. We begin our survey today with some thoughts on what lies ahead for foreign policy under George W Bush.
Mr Bush was elected president last November partly because he promised Americans something different after eight long years of Bill Clinton. He said his administration would put “nation first” rather than globalism above all else. It seemed unlikely then that Mr Bush could deliver much change so soon—especially since many people thought him too inexperienced even to run the White House let alone govern effectively.
But there were signs early on that things had changed. When Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in August 1990, President Bush Sr did little except talk loudly until Britain persuaded him otherwise. His son’s response to September 11th showed just how quickly events moved if you acted decisively enough. And while most observers still think that Mr Bush lacks experience compared with either Al Gore or Tony Blair, few doubt any longer whether he possesses courage—or indeed leadership qualities—in abundance.
This does not mean that everything will go smoothly between now and next year’s presidential election. There remain plenty of problems waiting to trip anyone up—including one called terrorism—and no shortage of critics ready to pounce should anything seem amiss. But already Washington looks very different place where it used to do business before.
For starters, relations with Europe appear set fairer than ever thanks largely to British prime minister Tony Blair—who himself appears happier working alongside someone whom he thinks shares similar values instead of having to fight against them every step of way—as well as France’s Jacques Chirac, Germany’s Gerhard Schroeder and Italy’s Silvio Berlusconi—all three men keenly aware that European unity depends upon close co-operation among themselves regardless of differences elsewhere around globe.
Indeed, although Europeans often complain bitterly whenever US troops invade another country—even though none live anywhere near continent—they tend nevertheless respect military strength especially given current state affairs across Middle East region. This means that despite occasional squabbles along road—from disagreements over trade barriers right down through issues concerning human rights abuses carried out during past wars—the transatlantic relationship remains solid foundation future prosperity throughout Western hemisphere.
Of course, nothing lasts forever—not least alliances forged hastily together amid crisis situations—but history suggests that unless major powers start fighting each others’ battles directly—which hasn’t happened yet—it stands good chance lasting peace prevailing everywhere sooner rather later provided everyone keeps talking calmly amongst ourselves whilst continuing work building bridges wherever possible…

Dog’s Nose Can Detect Cancer, Study Says
By JENNIFER CORBETT and RACHEL DOUGLAS | The New York Times News Service
A dog named Hope is trained to sniff out breast tumors. (Photo: AP)
NEW YORK — A new study suggests that dogs may be able to help doctors diagnose some cancers by detecting the scent of tumor cells in breath or blood.
The research was conducted at a veterinary hospital near Boston where 10-year-old German shepherd “Hope” has been training for years as an early detection tool with her human partner Dr. Amy McDaniel, who works there.
McDaniel said she had long suspected that animals could smell things humans cannot because they have more than one million olfactory receptors compared to about four hundred thousand on people.
She began working closely with veterinarians from Tufts University School of Veterinary Medicine after noticing how well their patients responded when given drugs based upon what scents were detected during routine exams.
In this case, it turned out that many pets suffering from chronic kidney disease showed signs only if certain chemicals called urea nitrogen compounds were present in urine samples taken before treatment.
“Animals are very good at picking up subtle changes,” Mc Daniel told reporters recently while showing off Hope outside the clinic which specializes in treating sick cats and dogs.
“She picks them right away.”
But even though other studies suggest that dogs’ noses might also pick up signals associated with lung, bladder and ovarian cancers among others; researchers say much work remains ahead including determining whether these findings will translate into improved medical care for humans too.
For now however scientists agree we still don’t know enough yet so let us hope someday soon our furry friends become part of everyday life again just like back then!

[ANS] A New Way To Make Solar Cells - 2007-10-30
A team of researchers at the University of California, Riverside has developed a method for making thin-film photovoltaic devices that could lead to cheaper and more efficient solar energy.
The research was published in Nature Materials on Oct. 21 by UC Riverside professor Hua Zhang , his graduate student Yujie Rong (first author), postdoctoral researcher Xiangfeng Duan from Peking University, China; and their colleagues: Zhenan Bao, associate director of Stanford's Institute for Polymer Research ; Xiaoyang Zhuo, assistant professor of chemistry at UCR; and Qian Wang, an undergraduate physics major who is now working as a scientist with Hewlett-Packard Co., Palo Alto, Calif .
Zhang said he hopes this work will help bring down costs associated with producing silicon-based PVs -- which are currently used commercially but have high manufacturing cost because they require large amounts of expensive materials such as polysilicon or glass substrates . The technology also requires complex processing steps involving multiple masks during fabrication.
In contrast, the technique described here uses inexpensive copper foil instead of costly glasses or polymers as substrate material. It can be fabricated using simple printing techniques without any mask required. This makes it possible to produce flexible plastic films containing thousands of tiny nanowires made up entirely of semiconductor compounds called chalcogenides.
Chalcogens include sulfur, selenium and tellurium, all elements found naturally occurring within Earth ' s crust. They form crystals when combined with other metals like cadmium, zinc, tin and indium. These semimetallic alloys exhibit unique electrical properties due to quantum confinement effects caused by small size of these nanostructures.

Biggest Ever Galaxy Found in Universe, Scientists Say 
By MALCOLM RITTER and MARCIA DUNN Associated Press Writers 
WASHINGTON (AP) -- Astronomers have found what may be one of the biggest galaxies ever seen. It's so big that it could contain more than a trillion stars.
The galaxy is about twice as large as our Milky Way galaxy but only half its age — just over 10 billion years old compared to some 13 or even 14 billion for ours. That means this new giant was born relatively recently by cosmic standards; scientists think most other massive galaxies were formed much earlier during an era called reionization when hydrogen atoms first became ionized after being created at the Big Bang.
"This object has been hiding from us," said astronomer Pieter van Dokkum with Yale University who led the research team announced Wednesday in Washington. He says they've known since last year there must exist such huge objects because their light would otherwise not reach Earth today without passing through them along the way.
But finding evidence had proved elusive until now. Van Dokkum presented his findings before hundreds gathered here for meetings sponsored by the American Association for the Advancement of Science.
He described how he used NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope to look back into space where no human eye can see. Using infrared wavelengths invisible to humans' eyesight, astronomers are able to peer beyond billions of miles away toward distant regions of early universe history.
Van Dokkum focused on two areas near each end of the constellation Eridanus which lies between Orion and Sagittarius. In both places, he saw bright spots surrounded by faint glow indicating something very far off indeed.
Using computer simulations based upon Einsteinian physics, researchers determined these points represented enormous masses packed tightly together within vast distances. They calculated the mass density inside those spaces exceeded anything else observed anywhere except perhaps around black holes.
They concluded the brightest spot represents a single supermassive elliptical galaxy containing several hundred million suns while another contains roughly three times as many. Both appear young enough to still retain gas clouds capable of forming additional generations of star clusters like we observe throughout the sky.
Astronomy experts say if confirmed, this discovery might help explain why certain types of quasars seem brighter than others despite having similar sizes. By David Shukman BBC News science correspondent 
The idea that you could talk on your mobile without using any wires or batteries has been around since at least as far back as the late 1970s.
But now it seems we may be getting closer than ever before. Researchers in Japan have developed an electronic device which can transmit sound through air and water with no need for electricity.
It works by sending out pulses of light from two tiny mirrors inside each other; one mirror reflects off its partner while another sends energy into surrounding matter such as glass or plastic.
This creates what are known as "optical resonators" (OR) within these materials, where waves bounce between them like ripples across a pond.
When this happens they create standing wave patterns similar to those found when tuning musical instruments.
These ORs act much like antennas but instead use optical rather than electrical signals so there is nothing to lose if something goes wrong during transmission.
In fact because all their components work together perfectly synchronously even small errors will not affect performance too badly although some researchers believe more sophisticated systems might eventually require greater precision.
So how does our new technology compare?

The idea that you could talk on your mobile without using any wires or batteries has been around since at least as far back as the late 1970s.
But now it seems we may be getting closer than ever before. Researchers in Japan have developed an electronic device which can transmit sound through air and water with no need for electricity.
It works by sending out pulses of light from two tiny mirrors inside each other; one mirror reflects off its partner while another sends energy into surrounding matter such as glass or plastic.
This creates what are known as "optical resonators" (OR) within these materials, where waves bounce between them like ripples across a pond.
When this happens they create standing wave patterns similar to those found when tuning musical instruments.
These ORs act much like antennas but instead use optical rather than electrical signals so there is nothing to lose if something goes wrong during transmission.
In fact because all their components work together perfectly synchronously even small errors will not affect performance too badly although some researchers believe more sophisticated systems might eventually require greater precision.
So how does our new technology compare?
Well unlike conventional wireless phones whose signal strength falls away rapidly over distance both devices operate effectively up until about half-way round Earth itself meaning users would only really notice problems travelling beyond say five miles inland towards mountainous regions.
And whereas most modern handsets rely upon radio frequencies being transmitted via satellites orbiting above us others still depend solely upon electromagnetic fields generated directly below ground level making underground tunnels ideal locations for communication networks capable transmitting voice messages instantly regardless whether anyone else was present nearby.
Of course neither system offers complete immunity against interference either due natural phenomena occurring outside human control nor deliberate attempts made deliberately designed specifically target specific individuals groups organisations etc..

Four Ways To Make A Better Battery
By:  David Biello  in Scientific American, March/April 2011 issue.
The lithium-ion batteries that power our cell phones and laptops are getting smaller but more powerful. But they still have some problems—like the fact that their anodes can’t hold as much charge or last nearly long enough for electric cars—and scientists around the world are working on new materials with which to build them. THE NEW WORLD ORDER (1)
AFTER a decade in which America's power has been challenged from without 
and within, it seems that its moment may have come again. In recent weeks,
the United States has shown itself to be not only strong but also wise--in 
its handling both of Iraq and North Korea; as well as generous towards other 
nations such as China or India who are trying hard to catch up with them;
as well as tough-minded about those like Iran whose ambitions threaten their own security.
America can now look forward confidently into an era when they will once more play leading roles at home and abroad.
In this issue we examine how far these changes might affect American life over coming years. We begin our survey today with some thoughts on what lies ahead for foreign policy under George W Bush.
Mr Bush was elected president last November partly because he promised Americans something different after eight long years of Bill Clinton. He said his administration would put “nation first” rather than globalism above all else. It seemed unlikely then that Mr Bush could deliver much change so soon—especially since many people thought him too inexperienced even to run the White House let alone govern effectively.
But there were signs early on that things had changed. When Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in August 1990, President Bush Sr did little except talk loudly until Britain persuaded him otherwise. His son’s response to September 11th showed just how quickly events moved if you acted decisively enough. And while most observers still think that Mr Bush lacks experience compared with either Al Gore or Tony Blair, few doubt any longer whether he possesses courage—or indeed leadership qualities—in abundance.
This does not mean that everything will go smoothly between now and next year’s presidential election. There remain plenty of problems waiting to trip anyone up—including one called terrorism—and no shortage of critics ready to pounce should anything seem amiss. But already Washington looks very different place where it used to do business before.
For starters, relations with Europe appear set fairer than ever thanks largely to British prime minister Tony Blair—who himself appears happier working alongside someone whom he thinks shares similar values instead of having to fight against them every step of way—as well as France’s Jacques Chirac, Germany’s Gerhard Schroeder and Italy’s Silvio Berlusconi—all three men keenly aware that European unity depends upon close co-operation among themselves regardless of differences elsewhere around globe.
Indeed, although Europeans often complain bitterly whenever US troops invade another country—even though none live anywhere near continent—they tend nevertheless respect military strength especially given current state affairs across Middle East region. This means that despite occasional squabbles along road—from disagreements over trade barriers right down through issues concerning human rights abuses carried out during past wars—the transatlantic relationship remains solid foundation future prosperity throughout Western hemisphere.
Of course, nothing lasts forever—not least alliances forged hastily together amid crisis situations—but history suggests that unless major powers start fighting each others’ battles directly—which hasn’t happened yet—it stands good chance lasting peace prevailing everywhere sooner rather later provided everyone keeps talking calmly amongst ourselves whilst continuing work building bridges wherever possible…

[ANS] A New Way To Make Solar Cells - 2007-10-30
A team of researchers at the University of California, Riverside has developed a method for making thin-film photovoltaic devices that could lead to cheaper and more efficient solar energy.
The research was published in Nature Materials on Oct. 21 by UC Riverside professor Hua Zhang , his graduate student Yujie Rong (first author), postdoctoral researcher Xiangfeng Duan from Peking University, China; and their colleagues: Zhenan Bao, associate director of Stanford's Institute for Polymer Research ; Xiaoyang Zhuo, assistant professor of chemistry at UCR; and Qian Wang, an undergraduate physics major who is now working as a scientist with Hewlett-Packard Co., Palo Alto, Calif .
Zhang said he hopes this work will help bring down costs associated with producing silicon-based PVs -- which are currently used commercially but have high manufacturing cost because they require large amounts of expensive materials such as polysilicon or glass substrates . The technology also requires complex processing steps involving multiple masks during fabrication.
In contrast, the technique described here uses inexpensive copper foil instead of costly glasses or polymers as substrate material. It can be fabricated using simple printing techniques without any mask required. This makes it possible to produce flexible plastic films containing thousands of tiny nanowires made up entirely of semiconductor compounds called chalcogenides.
Chalcogens include sulfur, selenium and tellurium, all elements found naturally occurring within Earth ' s crust. They form crystals when combined with other metals like cadmium, zinc, tin and indium. These semimetallic alloys exhibit unique electrical properties due to quantum confinement effects caused by small size of these nanostructures.
" We believe our approach may provide a low-cost alternative route toward fabricating next-generation organic electronics ," says co-author Professor Ba o, whose group specializes in developing novel electronic components based upon conducting polymer blends.

The first time I saw the new generation of washing machine robots was at an event in Tokyo.
